summary:
Georgia is dangerous for trans visitors, and the position has deteriorated sharply. In September 2024 the Parliament of Georgia adopted the law "On the Protection of Family Values and Minors", which bans legal gender recognition, transition-related healthcare, public LGBT assembly and the dissemination of "LGBT information". It is the harshest such legislative package in the region, and it closed the two routes — official documents and transition-related care — by which a trans visitor or resident would ordinarily manage daily life.

One day after the law passed, Kesaria Abramidze, a trans model and influencer and one of Georgia's best-known transgender women, was stabbed to death in her apartment in Tbilisi. German foreign-affairs committee chair Michael Roth and EU foreign policy chief Josep Borrell condemned the law as further derailing Georgia's EU path. AP reported in October 2024 that the killing, together with Russia-style "gay propaganda" legislation, was raising fears of hate crimes in the conservative South Caucasus nation.

Service access has contracted alongside the legal position. ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2025 records that the foreign agents law endangers LGBTI service provision, because organisations that refuse to register as "foreign agents" face fines and bankruptcy; that the anti-LGBTI law eroded trust and reduced the number of service applications; that large numbers of LGBTI people are fleeing the country and seeking asylum documentation; and that misinformation demonising the LGBTI community is spreading.

Paperwork mismatch is a long-standing trans-specific barrier. In May 2012 IWPR reported legal activists arguing that the law had to be changed to allow gender recognition, and that job applications become difficult when a person's gender identity does not match their official documents.

Public assembly is obstructed by the Interior Ministry as well as by far-right threat. In June 2019 the ministry declared that Tbilisi Pride could not take place in the planned city-centre locations "due to safety risks", for a programme running 18 to 23 June. Organisers reported a week of pressure from an unidentified government official to cancel the march, and far-right groups had vowed to thwart what was the country's first-ever pride.

The protection machinery is weak on paper as well as in practice. A report by WISG and partner organisations to the Council of Europe Committee of Ministers, dated 5 August 2024, calls for urgent action: effective investigations into anti-LGBTI violence, withdrawal of the proposed anti-LGBTI legislation, improved hate-crime data collection, and protection of LGBTI assembly and expression. The legislation was adopted the following month.
tangentialFactors:
The 2024 package follows a documented pattern of state obstruction of assembly rather than an isolated decision. The Interior Ministry's June 2019 refusal to permit the first Tbilisi Pride in city-centre locations, attributed to safety risks, came alongside pressure on organisers to cancel and open vows by far-right groups to stop the march.

Georgia's trajectory is being read against a neighbouring jurisdiction's model. AP's October 2024 reporting frames the anti-LGBTI measures as Russia-style "gay propaganda" laws stoking fear of hate crimes, and situates the killing of Kesaria Abramidze within a broader crackdown linked to the election period.

Foreign policy consequences follow the domestic record. Michael Roth and Josep Borrell's condemnation of the law as further derailing Georgia's EU path places the legislation inside the country's accession process, an external pressure point that has no bearing on day-to-day safety for a visitor on the ground.

The foreign agents law operates as adjacent turbulence even where it is not an LGBTI statute: the compliance burden it places on civil society is the mechanism through which LGBTI service provision is endangered, and the same registration regime supplies the channel through which misinformation about the community circulates.

Earlier documentation shows the document barrier predates the 2024 law. The 2012 findings on employment difficulties caused by mismatched paperwork are the baseline against which the outright ban on legal gender recognition should be read.
localsOnly:
Residents who need to change their legal gender lost the statutory basis for doing so when the September 2024 law took effect, alongside access to transition-related healthcare. The same statute removes public LGBT assembly, so organised community events cannot be held openly.

Employment remains a practical pressure point. ILGA-Europe reports that service applications have fallen since the anti-LGBTI law, reflecting eroded trust in institutions rather than reduced need, and that misinformation demonising the LGBTI community is circulating.

Emigration is occurring at scale. Large numbers of LGBTI people are leaving Georgia and seeking asylum documentation abroad, a measure of the domestic situation for residents who cannot relocate privately.

Service providers face a registration trap. Organisations that refuse to register as "foreign agents" under the foreign agents law risk fines and eventual bankruptcy, which constrains what help an LGBTI resident can obtain without exposing themselves.

Reporting and accountability are under-documented. WISG and partner organisations asked the Council of Europe Committee of Ministers on 5 August 2024 to press for effective investigations into anti-LGBTI violence and for improved hate-crime data collection, indicating that recorded figures understate the incidence of attacks.
outOfScopeNotes:
The specific penalties attached to the offences created by the September 2024 law are not stated in the sources available here; the ban's scope is documented, the sentencing range is unresolved.

Enforcement practice since adoption is not sourced. Whether the bans on legal gender recognition, transition-related healthcare and public assembly have been applied to visitors, and how frequently, cannot be determined from the material reviewed.

The status of the recommendations in the 5 August 2024 report to the Council of Europe Committee of Ministers is unresolved here; no follow-up or government response is available in this inventory.

Whether any administrative route to gender recognition survives in narrowed form, for example for documents issued abroad, is not addressed by these sources.

The employment and documentation findings date from 2012 and the assembly obstruction from 2019. Both are clearly dated, but current street-level practice in Tbilisi and other cities is not independently sourced beyond the 2024 material.

AP's headline framing of the measures as raising fears of hate crimes is a publication's own characterisation; the underlying killing is documented, a general rise in recorded hate-crime incidents is not quantified in this inventory.
